title: 2026-10-22_Tsunami_Kaiten_Incident_Response_Scenario_13c
description: Investigate and respond to a potential security incident involving the Tsunami/Kaiten malware family.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The network has experienced unusual activity that may indicate a compromise. Your task is to investigate and respond to this potential security incident involving the Tsunami/Kaiten malware family.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the target host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: target
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

Enter 'start' to begin the investigation.
levels.local_content:
You have SSH access to the target host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: target
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

Enter 'start' to begin the investigation

levels.title: Investigate Unusual Network Connections
levels.content: Investigate the unusual network connections on the target host. Identify and investigate an unauthorized or suspicious service running on the target host. Submit the service name as your answer.
levels.solution: Check the network connections and running services on the target host. The service name is tsunami.service.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by examining the active network connections and running services on the target host.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Look for any unusual or unauthorized services that might be running on the target host.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'systemctl list-units --type=service' to list all active services.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot. Identify persistence mechanisms (e.g., systemd, cron, scheduled task). Submit the service name as your answer.
levels.solution: Examine the systemd services and timers on the target host. The service name is kaiten.service.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Persistence mechanisms often involve systemd services, cron jobs, or scheduled tasks.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Focus on systemd services and timers that might be responsible for automatically starting the suspicious service.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'systemctl list-unit-files --type=service' to list all systemd services.

levels.title: Investigate File Transfers
levels.content: Investigate the file transfers between the target and next-target hosts. Identify file transfers or remote execution used to move between hosts. Submit the service name as your answer.
levels.solution: Check the systemd services and logs related to file transfers on the target host. The service name is payload-transfer.service.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: File transfers and remote execution can often be identified through systemd services and logs.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Look for systemd services that might be responsible for transferring files or executing commands remotely.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Use the command 'journalctl -u payload-transfer.service' to check the logs of the payload-transfer.service.
